snapshots.name: Thucydides
snapshots.body: The Athenian who wrote this. He began at the moment the war broke out, judging it would be greater than any before, and he says plainly what he did about the speeches: he made the speakers say what the occasion called for, keeping as close as he could to the general sense of what was really said. The narrative he tested by the most severe scrutiny he could manage, since eye-witnesses of the same event do not agree. He wrote it, he says, not as an essay to win the applause of the moment but as a possession for all time.

snapshots.name: Homer
snapshots.body: Thucydides’s chief witness for the age before the war, and his chief problem with it. snapshots.name: Perdiccas
snapshots.body: Alexander’s son and king of the Macedonians, turned from an old Athenian friend and ally into an enemy because Athens allied with his brother Philip and with Derdas. He worked on Lacedaemon and on Corinth to get Potidaea into revolt, persuaded the Chalcidians to demolish their seaboard towns and settle inland at Olynthus on land he gave them round Lake Bolbe, and changed sides twice in one campaign — deputing Iolaus to command the cavalry he had just brought back to the Potidaean side.

snapshots.name: Perdiccas
snapshots.body: King of the Macedonians and nobody’s reliable ally. Reconciled to Athens and given Therme back, he at once joined Phormio against the Chalcidians; he had promised Sitalces something for the reconciliation and never paid it, and Sitalces came down with a hundred and fifty thousand men and the pretender Amyntas in his baggage. Perdiccas bought the retreat by promising his sister to Sitalces’s nephew — and gave Stratonice to Seuthes as promised. He also sent a thousand Macedonians to Cnemus in Acarnania without the Athenians knowing, and they arrived too late.

snapshots.name: Aristeus
snapshots.body: Adimantus’s son, always a steady friend of the Potidaeans — most of the Corinthian volunteers went out of love for him. Made general of all the infantry, he won with his own wing and lost with the rest, and got most of his men into Potidaea at a run along the breakwater through the sea. When the investment closed he advised all but five hundred to sail out so the provisions would last, offered to stay himself, could not persuade them, and slipped past the guardships alone to carry on the war from Chalcidice. Not the admiral beaten at Epidamnus.

snapshots.name: Aristeus
snapshots.body: Adimantus’s son, the prime mover at Potidaea and in the Thracian towns, who went with the Lacedaemonian envoys to the King to ask for money. Sadocus seized them in Thrace and handed them over, and the Athenians killed them all the same day without a trial and threw the bodies into a pit — afraid that if Aristeus got away he would do them still more harm.

snapshots.name: Phormio
snapshots.body: Asopius’s son, who brought sixteen hundred Athenian infantry round to the Pallene side of Potidaea, fixed his headquarters at Aphytis, and raised the works nobody had dared to raise — closing the investment on both sides. He then used the same force to ravage Chalcidice and Bottica and take some of the towns.

snapshots.name: Phormio
snapshots.body: Asopius’s son, with twenty ships at Naupactus against forty-seven. He sailed round the Peloponnesian circle until the morning wind came down the gulf and their oars fouled, then gave the signal and took twelve ships. Six days later, with seventy-seven against his twenty, he was forced along the shore and lost nine of them — until one Athenian ship rounded a moored merchantman, rammed the Leucadian chasing her, and turned the day. He told his men beforehand that the Peloponnesians feared their irrational audacity more than they would have feared a proportionate force.

snapshots.name: Archidamus
snapshots.body: The Lacedaemonian king with the reputation of being wise and moderate, who told the assembly what a war against a distant people with money, ships, horses and tributary allies would cost: they were inferior at sea, far worse off for money, and could not end it by burning fields. He asked for embassies and two or three years of preparation, said he feared they would leave the war as a legacy to their children, and was voted down.

snapshots.name: Archidamus
snapshots.body: Zeuxidamus’s son, king of Lacedaemon and leader of the invasions. He told the assembled generals that confidence in an army of invasion must be matched by caution, wasted the first campaign in front of Oenoe hoping Athens would submit while her land was untouched — for which the army blamed him — and then sat at Acharnae to see whether three thousand Acharnian hoplites would force a battle on the rest of the city. At Plataea he heard the envoys out, offered them neutrality or a receipt for their land, and when they refused called the gods and heroes of their own country to witness that he had made many fair proposals and had not succeeded.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Sthenelaidas
snapshots.body: The ephor who answered Archidamus — the Athenians had said a great deal in praise of themselves and nowhere denied the wrong, so they deserved double punishment, for having ceased to be good and for having become bad. He then refused to judge the shouting and made the assembly divide by walking to two sides of the room, so that they would have to declare themselves and their ardour for war would rise.

snapshots.name: Leotychides
snapshots.body: King of the Lacedaemonians and commander of the Hellenes at Mycale, who went home with the Peloponnesian allies while the Athenians and the Ionians stayed to take Sestos.

snapshots.name: Themistocles
snapshots.body: The commander at Salamis, whom Thucydides calls the ablest judge of a sudden crisis and the best prophet of a distant future that ever was — genius by native ability, neither shaped nor supplemented by study. He got Athens walled by going to Sparta himself and stalling there while the whole city, women and children included, tore down buildings for materials; he finished Piraeus, told Athens to stick to the sea, and laid the foundations of the empire.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Themistocles
snapshots.body: The commander at Salamis and the ablest man of his time, in Thucydides’s judgement, at meeting an emergency. Implicated in the inquiry into Pausanias’s Medism, already ostracised and living at Argos, he was hunted through the Peloponnese, refused by Corcyra, and took sanctuary at the hearth of Admetus the Molossian with the king’s child in his arms. He reached Artaxerxes by letter, asked a year’s grace to learn Persian, and ended governor of Magnesia — fifty talents a year for bread, Lampsacus for wine, Myos for the rest. Disease killed him, though there is a story of poison; his bones were brought home secretly, since it is against the law to bury a traitor in Attica.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Pausanias
snapshots.body: Cleombrotus’s son, sent out as commander-in-chief of the Hellenes, who took Cyprus and Byzantium and then lost the command by playing the autocrat: the Ionians and the newly liberated went over to the Athenians to be rid of him, and Sparta recalled him on charges of which Medism was the best founded and acquitted him of it.

snapshots.name: Pausanias
snapshots.body: The hero of Plataea, and the reason the confederacy changed hands. Sent the King his captured kinsmen with a cover story and a letter offering to marry his daughter and make Sparta and Hellas subject to him; came back from Byzantium in Median dress with a Persian table and a bodyguard of Medes and Egyptians. He had put his own couplet on the tripod at Delphi and had it erased, was intriguing with the Helots with promises of freedom and citizenship, and was undone by his own courier, who counterfeited the seal and found the order for his death. He ran for the temple of the goddess of the Brazen House, was walled in, and was carried out to die on the threshold; Delphi made Sparta move the tomb and give the goddess two bronze statues for the one body.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Dorkis
snapshots.body: Sent out with a few others and a small force to replace Pausanias, and found the allies no longer willing to grant Lacedaemon the supremacy. He left, and Sparta sent no one after him.

snapshots.body: Psammetichus’s son, a Libyan king of the Libyans on the Egyptian border with his headquarters at Marea, who raised almost all Egypt against Artaxerxes and called in the Athenians — and who was betrayed, captured and crucified.

snapshots.body: Inaros’s father.

snapshots.name: Artaxerxes
snapshots.body: Xerxes’s son, newly come to the throne when Themistocles wrote to him; the king Egypt revolted from.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Amyrtaeus
snapshots.body: The king in the marshes, whom the Persians could not take because of the size of the marsh and because the marshmen are the most warlike of the Egyptians — and who afterwards got sixty of Cimon’s ships.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Leocrates
snapshots.body: Stroebus’s son, who commanded the landing and the siege after the great sea-battle off Aegina.

snapshots.name: Stroebus
snapshots.body: Leocrates’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Myronides
snapshots.body: Who marched into the Megarid with the old men and the boys left in the city, fought the Corinthians to a draw, and when they came back twelve days later to set up their own trophy cut off the party setting it up and stoned a whole detachment to death in a walled field. Sixty-two days after Tanagra he beat the Boeotians at Oenophyta.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Nicomedes
snapshots.body: Cleombrotus’s son, acting for the boy king Pleistoanax, who brought fifteen hundred Lacedaemonians and ten thousand allies to the help of Doris and then had to sit in Boeotia deciding which way home — encouraged by a party in Athens that wanted the democracy and the Long Walls stopped.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Pleistoanax
snapshots.body: Pausanias’s son, king of the Lacedaemonians: a minor when Nicomedes acted for him, and in command himself of the invasion that reached Eleusis and Thrius and went no further.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Pleistoanax
snapshots.body: Pausanias’s son and king of Lacedaemon, whose invasion fourteen years earlier had turned back at Eleusis and Thria — which cost him his exile, since it was thought he had been bribed to retreat. While Archidamus’s army was on the same ground, the Athenians remembered it and still hoped he would go no further.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Tolmides
snapshots.body: Tolmaeus’s son, who sailed round the Peloponnese, burnt the Lacedaemonian dockyard, took Chalcis and beat the Sicyonians — and who was caught at Coronea on the way home from Chaeronea by the Boeotian exiles, and lost Boeotia with the battle.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Tolmaeus
snapshots.body: Tolmides’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Megabazus
snapshots.body: The Persian sent to Lacedaemon with money to buy an invasion of Attica and draw the Athenians out of Egypt, and recalled with what was left of it when the money was simply being wasted. Not Megabuzus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Megabuzus
snapshots.body: Zopyrus’s son, sent into Egypt with a large army instead: he beat the Egyptians in the field, drove the Hellenes out of Memphis, penned them on Prosopitis for a year and a half, and then drained the canal, left their ships dry, and marched across on foot. Not Megabazus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Zopyrus
snapshots.body: Megabuzus’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Orestes
snapshots.body: Echecratidas’s son, the Thessalian king in exile who persuaded Athens to restore him — and went home with them again, the expedition having accomplished nothing because of the Thessalian cavalry.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Echecratidas
snapshots.body: Orestes’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Pericles
snapshots.body: Xanthippus’s son, who took a thousand men from Pegae to Sicyon and Acarnania, brought the army back from Euboea when Megara revolted and then subdued Euboea outright, and commanded the forty-four ships that beat the Samians off Tragia.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Pericles
snapshots.body: Xanthippus’s son, the most powerful man of his time and the foremost Athenian statesman, ablest alike in counsel and in action. He was connected with the Cylonian curse on his mother’s side, which is why Sparta’s first embassy demanded the accursed be driven out — not expecting to succeed, but to make his countrymen think the war his bad luck. He answered the ultimatum with no concession: the trifle of the Megara decree, he said, contains the whole trial of their resolve; Athens should think of herself as an island, guard the sea and the city, and mourn the loss of men rather than of houses and land, because men gain houses and land and not the reverse. What he feared, he said, was Athenian blunders rather than the enemy’s designs.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Pericles
snapshots.body: The first citizen of Athens, whose funeral speech for the first of the war’s dead calls the city the school of Hellas and says that heroes have the whole earth for their tomb. He would not let the army out while Archidamus burned Acharnae, would not call an assembly while anger was in the ascendant, and handed over his own estate to the state in case Archidamus spared it out of friendship. They fined him, and then elected him general again. He outlived the outbreak by two years and six months, and told them to wait quietly, attend to the navy, attempt no new conquests and risk nothing — advice they did the opposite of. What was nominally a democracy became in his hands government by the first citizen.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Xanthippus
snapshots.body: Pericles’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Pissuthnes
snapshots.body: Hystaspes’s son, satrap of Sardis, who took the Athenian garrison and its commanders off the Samian rebels.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hystaspes
snapshots.body: Pissuthnes’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Stesagoras
snapshots.body: Who left Samos with five ships to bring up the Phoenician fleet — which is why Pericles was off Caria when the Samians broke out and held their own waters for fourteen days.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hagnon
snapshots.body: One of the three commanders of the forty ships that reinforced the siege of Samos.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hagnon
snapshots.body: Nicias’s son, who took Pericles’s own force to the Chalcidians and Potidaea and brought the plague with him: he lost one thousand and fifty out of four thousand heavy infantry in about forty days, achieved nothing worthy of his preparations, and took his ships home. He went out again with Sitalces’s expedition as the Athenian general — for a fleet that never came.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: Tlepolemus
snapshots.body: Who brought twenty more ships to Samos with Anticles.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Anticles
snapshots.body: Tlepolemus’s colleague.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cylon
snapshots.body: An Olympic victor of good birth and powerful position, married to a daughter of Theagenes of Megara, who asked at Delphi and was told to seize the Acropolis at the grand festival of Zeus. He took it during the Olympic festival in the Peloponnese, never asking which festival the god meant and never being told — the Athenians have a grand festival of Zeus Meilichios of their own, the Diasia. He and his brother got away; the rest starved at the altar, were raised on a promise of no harm, and were killed. The men who killed them were the accursed, they and their descendants, and driving them out was the first thing Sparta demanded of Athens before the war.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Theagenes
snapshots.body: Tyrant of Megara, whose daughter Cylon married and whose force he used.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cleomenes
snapshots.body: Of Lacedaemon, who with an Athenian faction drove the accursed out a second time: the living expelled, the bones of the dead taken up.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Gongylus
snapshots.body: The Eretrian whom Pausanias put in charge of Byzantium and the captured kinsmen of the King, and who carried the letter offering to make Sparta and Hellas subject to Persia.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Artabazus
snapshots.body: Pharnaces’s son, sent down to the sea to replace Megabates in the satrapy of Daskylion, to show Pausanias the royal seal, and to carry the King’s business with him with all care and fidelity.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Pharnaces
snapshots.body: Artabazus’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Megabates
snapshots.body: The governor of the satrapy of Daskylion whom Artabazus was sent to replace.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Pleistarchus
snapshots.body: Leonidas’s son, the boy king Pausanias was regent for, and his first cousin.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Leonidas
snapshots.body: Pleistarchus’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Admetus
snapshots.body: The Molossian king, not on friendly terms with Themistocles, who was out when Themistocles arrived; his wife told the suppliant to take their child in his arms and sit by the hearth. He raised him up with the boy still in his arms, refused the Lacedaemonians whatever they said, and sent him overland to the other sea.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Ramphias
snapshots.body: First-named of the three ambassadors who brought the Lacedaemonian ultimatum: not a word on any of the old subjects, only that Lacedaemon wished the peace to continue and there was no reason it should not, if Athens would leave the Hellenes independent.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Melesippus
snapshots.body: The second of the three ambassadors.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Agesander
snapshots.body: The third of the three ambassadors.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Zeus
snapshots.body: Whose grand festival Cylon was told to wait for and did not identify — the Athenians have one of their own, to Zeus Meilichios the Gracious, kept outside the city at the Diasia with bloodless offerings. It is his suppliant at Ithome that an old oracle told Lacedaemon to release.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hera
snapshots.body: In whose temple at Corcyra the Epidamnian ambassadors sat as suppliants and were dismissed empty-handed.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Apollo
snapshots.body: The god at Delphi, who told Epidamnus to hand the city to Corinth, told Cylon to take the Acropolis at the grand festival of Zeus without saying which, told Lacedaemon that if they put their whole strength into the war victory would be theirs and that he himself would be with them invoked or not, and ordered Pausanias’s tomb moved to the place of his death. His temple stands at Actium, and Polycrates gave him Rhenea.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Poseidon
snapshots.body: From whose temple at Taenarus the Lacedaemonians raised the Helot suppliants and led them away and killed them — for which they believe the great earthquake at Sparta was retribution, and which the Athenians told them to drive out as a curse of their own.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Athenians
snapshots.body: Whose growth in power, and the alarm it inspired in Lacedaemon, Thucydides gives as the real cause of the war — the cause most kept out of sight in formal speech. Never displaced from Attica because the soil was poor, they laid aside their arms first, took to the sea after the Mede, and turned the confederacy into an empire.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Athenians
snapshots.body: Whose country population came into the city and camped in the temples and the towers, and among whom the plague then broke out — fever, thirst, and a despair that took away the power of resistance the moment a man felt himself sickening. The doctors died thickest, because they visited the sick most. Men who had nothing succeeded to the property of men who had everything, and spent it quickly; burial rites collapsed; and nobody expected to live to be tried for anything. An old verse said a Dorian war would come and a plague with it, and they argued about whether the word had been plague or dearth.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: The Lacedaemonians
snapshots.body: Slow to go to war except under necessity, with the same form of government for more than four hundred years and no tyrants; they put down the tyrannies of the rest of Hellas, led the alliance against the Mede, and exacted no tribute from their allies, only oligarchies. The Corinthians tell them to their faces that they are the only Hellenes who are inactive, and who defend themselves not by doing anything but by looking as though they might.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Peloponnesians
snapshots.body: Farmers without funds private or public, without experience of long wars overseas, and without the single council-chamber that prompt action needs — a diet of many peoples in which each state has an equal vote and pushes its own ends, so that nothing is done. That is Pericles’s account of them; their own is that they have numbers, experience, obedience, and the temple funds at Olympia and Delphi to hire away Athenian sailors with.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Corinthians
snapshots.body: Set on an isthmus and a commercial hub from time immemorial, the first to build galleys in Hellas and the first Hellenes to fight a sea-battle. They took over Epidamnus from a colony that despised them, lost at Leukimme, claimed the victory at Sybota, and canvassed the Peloponnese city by city for the war — speaking last at both congresses, after letting the other speakers inflame the room.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Corcyraeans
snapshots.body: Wealthy enough to stand comparison with the richest in Hellas, proud of a naval reputation they trace to the Phaeacians, and so placed that foreign ships must put in at them while they need not sail to anyone. They refused their own colonists, refused their mother city arbitration only after the siege was laid, and came to Athens with the offer of a hundred and twenty galleys and an argument about where the coming war would be fought.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Hellenes
snapshots.body: Thucydides’s word for the Greeks as one people: the name did not exist before Hellen, Homer never uses it of all of them, and it was long in attaching itself to the whole. All of them were drawn into this war sooner or later, though some at first stayed neutral.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Potidaeans
snapshots.body: A Corinthian colony on the isthmus of Pallene and tributary allies of Athens, ordered to raze the wall facing Pallene, give hostages and dismiss the Corinthian magistrates — and who revolted instead, with the Chalcidians and Bottiaeans, on a Lacedaemonian promise to invade Attica.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Epidamnians
snapshots.body: Whose city on the Ionic gulf grew large and then tore itself apart: the commons expelled the nobles, the nobles joined the barbarians and plundered them by sea and land, and their embassy to Corcyra was dismissed empty-handed from the temple of Hera. Delphi told them to give the city to Corinth.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Taulantians
snapshots.body: An Illyrian people, the barbarian neighbours of Epidamnus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Illyrians
snapshots.body: Whose help the Corcyraeans enlisted for the siege of Epidamnus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Ambraciots
snapshots.body: Who sent volunteer settlers and troops to Epidamnus, eight ships for the convoy and twenty-seven for the fleet, and held the right wing with the Megarians at Sybota.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Leucadians
snapshots.body: Whose city was a Corinthian colony: they sent settlers to Epidamnus and ten ships twice, and had their territory ravaged by the Corcyraeans for it.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Megarians
snapshots.body: Who left the Lacedaemonian alliance over a boundary war Corinth forced on them, were given long walls and an Athenian garrison, revolted and cut the garrison off — and who came to the congress with a long list of grievances, chief of them exclusion from the ports of the empire and the market of Athens. The decree excluding them was the one thing that could still have averted the war.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Aeginetans
snapshots.body: Who sent no formal representatives to the congress for fear of Athens and were in private among the most insistent advocates for war, claiming Athens had denied them the independence the treaty guaranteed.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Aeginetans
snapshots.body: Expelled from Aegina with their wives and children in the first summer of the war, as the chief agents in bringing it on — and because the island lay too close to the Peloponnese to be left in their hands. Lacedaemon gave them Thyrea, partly out of the obligation they had put her under at the time of the earthquake and the Helot revolt; the rest scattered over Hellas.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: The Samians
snapshots.body: For whom Ameinocles built the first four ships, and who went to war with Miletus over Priene, were given a democracy, stole back their hostages from Lemnos, revolted, and held their own waters for fourteen days before a nine-month siege ended it.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Milesians
snapshots.body: Beaten by Samos over Priene, and the complainants who brought Athens into the Samian war.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Thebans
snapshots.body: Asked for money toward the Epidamnus convoy; and the people whose city had given the Mede his base of operations, which is the argument Sparta used against walls.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Thebans
snapshots.body: Whose Boeotarchs took three hundred men into Plataea in peacetime, because they foresaw the war and wanted to surprise an old enemy before it began. They would not kill the opposite faction as the traitors wanted, made a conciliatory proclamation instead, and lost the whole party. The relieving force was held up by a river swollen with the night’s rain and arrived to find them dead.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Identity clarification released at the end of the reviewed source paragraph.

snapshots.name: The Phliasians
snapshots.body: Asked for money toward the convoy.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Eleans
snapshots.body: Asked for hulls as well as money; the Corcyraeans burnt Cyllene, their harbour, for it.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Sicyonians
snapshots.body: Whose envoys went with the Corcyraeans to Corinth, who were beaten by Pericles at Sicyon and by Tolmides before him, and who were let into Megara before the revolt.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Chalcidians
snapshots.body: Of the Thracian seaboard, who joined the Potidaean revolt and, at Perdiccas’s urging, demolished their own towns and moved inland to Olynthus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Bottiaeans
snapshots.body: Who joined the revolt with the Chalcidians and the Potidaeans.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Macedonians
snapshots.body: Perdiccas’s people, whose six hundred horse followed Philip and Pausanias on the Athenian side at Potidaea and then rode back to the Athenians when the battle was decided.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Thracians
snapshots.body: Who cut the ten thousand Athenian settlers off at Drabescus, taking the settlement at Nine Ways for an act of war.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Carians
snapshots.body: Great pirates who colonized most of the islands, expelled from the Cyclades by Minos; more than half the graves opened when Athens purified Delos were theirs, known by the weapons and the manner of burial they still use.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Phoenicians
snapshots.body: Islanders and pirates with the Carians; afterwards the King’s navy, which reduced the islands for Darius, lost two hundred ships at the Eurymedon, and was always expected and sometimes never came.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Pelasgians
snapshots.body: The name the country chiefly went by before Hellen, and the stock the Greek language branched off from.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Boeotians
snapshots.body: Driven out of Arne by the Thessalians sixty years after Ilium and settled in the Cadmeis; beaten at Oenophyta and masters again after Coronea. Homer gives their ships a hundred and twenty men each, the maximum in the catalogue.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Thessalians
snapshots.body: Who drove the Boeotians out of Arne; whose cavalry went over to the Lacedaemonians during the battle at Tanagra; and whose horse kept the Athenians inside their camp at Pharsalus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Dorians
snapshots.body: Who with the Heraclids became masters of the Peloponnese twenty years after the Boeotian resettlement, and whose settlement in Lacedaemon was followed by faction for an unparalleled length of time.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Ionians
snapshots.body: The colonies Athens sent out when Attica grew too small, whose golden grasshoppers and linen came from Athens; they built naval strength under Cyrus, were the first to ask Athens to take the lead against Pausanias, and are the people a Dorian city is being besieged by, which the Corinthians call a complete reversal of the natural order.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Heraclids
snapshots.body: Who killed Eurystheus in Attica and, with the Dorians, became masters of the Peloponnese; Phalius the founder of Epidamnus was of the family.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Mycenaeans
snapshots.body: Who feared the Heraclids and wanted Atreus to take the sceptre.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Trojans
snapshots.body: Who held the field for ten years because the invaders were always dispersed for piracy and farming, and were always a match for the detachment left on duty.

snapshots.name: The Medes
snapshots.body: The invader of the two invasions, and the measure Thucydides sets this war against: the Median War was the greatest event of past times and was settled in two sea-battles and two land-battles. The rock the barbarian was wrecked on, the Corinthians tell Sparta, was himself.

snapshots.name: The Persians
snapshots.body: Whose grandees’ quarters were the few houses left standing in Athens, and who held the White Castle at Memphis and Sestos and Byzantium until they were taken.

snapshots.name: The Phocians
snapshots.body: Who made an expedition against Doris, the original homeland of the Lacedaemonians, and were made to give the town back; Athens put the temple at Delphi into their hands.

snapshots.name: The Locrians
snapshots.body: The Ozolian Locrians, who still carry weapons in the old piratical way and from whom Athens took Naupactus; and the Opuntian Locrians, a hundred of whose richest men were taken as hostages after Oenophyta.

snapshots.name: The Acarnanians
snapshots.body: Invaded by land and threatened by sea, they made no combined resistance but stayed to defend their own homes — and the Stratians alone broke the Chaonians with ambushes and then slung at the Hellenic divisions from a distance, which is the kind of warfare Thucydides says they excel at.

snapshots.name: The Egyptians
snapshots.body: Most of whom revolted from Artaxerxes under Inaros and were beaten back into subjection — except the marshmen, who are the most warlike of them and whose king in the marshes could not be taken.

snapshots.name: The Helots
snapshots.body: Most of them descendants of the old Messenians enslaved in the famous war, which is why they all came to be called Messenians. They seceded to Ithome after the earthquake; Pausanias promised them freedom and citizenship to join him; and the suppliants raised from the temple of Poseidon at Taenarus and killed were Helots.

snapshots.name: The Messenians
snapshots.body: The name all the Helots came to carry, because most of them descended from the Messenians enslaved in the famous war; the rebels at Ithome held out ten years and were let out of the Peloponnese on condition of never setting foot in it again.

snapshots.name: The Messenians
snapshots.body: Settled by Athens at Naupactus after Ithome, and now the garrison that marched along the shore beside Phormio’s ships — and that waded into the sea in armour to board the disabled Athenian hulls the Peloponnesians were towing away, and took them back.

snapshots.body: Leontiades’s son, a man of great influence at Thebes, through whom the traitors in Plataea had made their arrangements — and one of the hundred and eighty prisoners the Plataeans put to death.

snapshots.name: Cecrops
snapshots.body: Under whom, and the first kings after him, Attica was a country of independent townships.

snapshots.name: Theseus
snapshots.body: The king of equal intelligence and power who abolished the council-chambers and magistrates of the smaller Attic cities and merged them into one council-chamber and town hall at Athens, leaving a great state behind him. snapshots.name: Brasidas
snapshots.body: Tellis’s son. In command of a guard in Laconia when the Athenians assaulted Methone, he ran a hundred heavy infantry straight through an army scattered over the country, lost a few men getting in, and saved the place — the first officer in the war to be publicly commended at Sparta. He was sent out afterwards as one of the three commissioners to stiffen Cnemus’s fleet, and was in the party that talked itself out of the raid on Piraeus. The older translation misprints him Bradidas once.

snapshots.name: Cleopompus
snapshots.body: Clinias’s son, who took thirty ships round Locris and Euboea, sacked places on the coast, took hostages from Thronium and beat the Locrians at Alope — and afterwards went with Hagnon to Potidaea and the Chalcidians.

snapshots.body: Pythes’s son, an Abderite whose sister was married to Sitalces. Athens had counted him an enemy and now made him her proxenus and sent for him: he brought in the Thracian alliance, got Sitalces’s son Sadocus made an Athenian citizen, and reconciled Athens with Perdiccas.

snapshots.body: Teres’s son and king of the Thracians, whose alliance Athens bought with a citizenship for his son and the return of Therme to Perdiccas. He came down into Macedonia with a hundred and fifty thousand men, a third of them horse, and frightened every people between Thermopylae and the Danube — and then, with no provisions and bad weather, took his nephew’s advice and went home after thirty days, having achieved none of it.

snapshots.body: Sitalces’s father, the first to build the great Odrysian kingdom out of a Thrace that was mostly independent. Thucydides is at pains to say he is in no way related to the Tereus of the nightingale story: different part of Thrace, different name.

snapshots.name: Xenophon
snapshots.body: Euripides’s son, first-named of the three Athenian generals who took Potidaea’s capitulation, and afterwards the commander beaten and killed at Spartolus.

snapshots.body: Xenophon the general’s father.

snapshots.name: Hestiodorus
snapshots.body: Aristocleides’s son, the second of the three generals at Potidaea.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Aristocleides
snapshots.body: Hestiodorus’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Phanomachus
snapshots.body: Callimachus’s son, the third of the three generals at Potidaea — blamed at home, with his colleagues, for granting terms without instructions.

snapshots.name: Callimachus
snapshots.body: Phanomachus’s father. Not Learchus’s father.

snapshots.name: Cnemus
snapshots.body: The Spartan high admiral: he ravaged Zacynthus and got nowhere, slipped past Phormio into the gulf with a thousand heavy infantry and a barbarian army, lost the Chaonians to an ambush at Stratus, and had three commissioners sent out in anger to stiffen him after his fleet was beaten in the Crissaean gulf.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Photys
snapshots.body: One of the two members of the Chaonian royal family entrusted with the chieftainship for the year; the Chaonians have no king.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Nicanor
snapshots.body: The other Chaonian chieftain of the year.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Sabylinthus
snapshots.body: Guardian of the boy king Tharyps, who led the Molossians and Atintanians into Acarnania.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Tharyps
snapshots.body: The Molossian king, still a minor, for whom Sabylinthus acted.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Oroedus
snapshots.body: King of the Paravaei, who brought them into Acarnania and was given the thousand Orestians to command as well.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Antiochus
snapshots.body: King of the Orestians, who sent a thousand of them under Oroedus rather than lead them himself. The older translation misprints him Antichus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Machaon
snapshots.body: One of the three Corinthian commanders of the forty-seven ships Phormio broke in the mouth of the Crissaean gulf.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Isocrates
snapshots.body: The second Corinthian commander.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Agatharchidas
snapshots.body: The third Corinthian commander.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Timocrates
snapshots.body: One of the three Lacedaemonian commissioners sent out in anger after the first defeat. He was aboard the Leucadian that an Athenian ship sank off a merchantman at Naupactus, killed himself when she went down, and was washed up in the harbour. Not Timoxenus’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Lycophron
snapshots.body: The third of the three Lacedaemonian commissioners, with Timocrates and Brasidas.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Nicias
snapshots.body: A Cretan of Gortys and the Athenians’ proxenus, who talked twenty ships out of joining Phormio and into attacking Cydonia — really to oblige the Polichnitans next door. Bad weather kept them in Crete through the battle.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Amyntas
snapshots.body: Philip’s son, whom Sitalces brought with him and intended for the throne of Macedonia; Idomene, Gortynia and Atalanta came over out of attachment to him.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Seuthes
snapshots.body: Spardacus’s son, Sitalces’s nephew and highest officer, and afterwards his successor, who raised the Odrysian tribute to four hundred talents. Perdiccas secretly bought him with the promise of his sister, and he advised the retreat; Perdiccas gave him Stratonice as promised.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Spardacus
snapshots.body: Seuthes’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Stratonice
snapshots.body: Perdiccas’s sister, promised to Seuthes with a rich dowry for the advice that ended Sitalces’s invasion, and given to him afterwards.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Archelaus
snapshots.body: Perdiccas’s son, who on his accession built most of the strongholds the country has, cut straight roads, and did more for the kingdom’s horses and heavy infantry than the eight kings before him together.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cynes
snapshots.body: Theolytus’s son, whom Phormio restored to Coronta.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Theolytus
snapshots.body: Cynes’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Alcmaeon
snapshots.body: Amphiaraus’s son, told by Apollo in his wanderings after killing his mother that he would have no release until he found land that had not been seen by the sun at the time of the murder. He settled on the Achelous’s new deposits by Oeniadae and named the country after his son Acarnan.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Acarnan
snapshots.body: Alcmaeon’s son, from whom Acarnania is named.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Odrysians
snapshots.body: Teres’s kingdom and Sitalces’s, whose empire ran from Abdera to the Danube and inland thirteen days’ journey, and whose custom was the opposite of the Persian one: more disgrace in refusing a present than in asking for one and being refused. Nothing could be done among them without a present.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Chaonians
snapshots.body: A nation with no king, led by two of the royal family for a year at a time, and with the highest reputation for courage on that part of the mainland. They would not wait to make camp at Stratus, rushed the town for the sole glory of it, and were cut to pieces from the city and the ambushes.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Thesprotians
snapshots.body: Who came with the Chaonians into Acarnania and, like them, have no king.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Atintanians
snapshots.body: Whom Sabylinthus led into Acarnania with the Molossians.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Paravaeans
snapshots.body: Who came under their own king Oroedus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Orestians
snapshots.body: A thousand of them, subjects of King Antiochus, who put them under Oroedus’s command.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Amphilochians
snapshots.body: Whose Argos was founded by Amphilochus and who learned their Hellenic speech from the Ambraciots they invited in — and were then expelled by them, upon which they joined the Acarnanians, called in Athens, and got the town back.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Agraeans
snapshots.body: Through whose country the Achelous runs on its way to the Acarnanian plain.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Stratians
snapshots.body: Of the Acarnanian capital, who saw how the invading divisions had strung out, set ambushes round the town, broke the Chaonians between the city and the ambushes, and then slung at the Hellenes from a distance — which, Thucydides says, is the kind of warfare the Acarnanians excel at.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Getae
snapshots.body: Beyond Haemus, who border on the Scythians and are armed like them, all mounted archers; they supplied more of Sitalces’s cavalry than anyone but the Odrysians.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Dii
snapshots.body: The independent hill Thracian swordsmen of Mount Rhodope, the most warlike of Sitalces’s infantry, some of whom came as mercenaries and some as volunteers.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Agrianes
snapshots.body: One of the Paeonian tribes in Sitalces’s empire, on its edge, with the Strymon running through their country.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Laeaeans
snapshots.body: The Paeonian tribe at the inland limit of the Odrysian empire, where it ends and the independent Paeonians begin.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Paeonians
snapshots.body: Some of them in the Odrysian empire and some independent; Sitalces cut his road to Macedonia through their timber on an earlier campaign against them.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Triballi
snapshots.body: Independent, and the neighbours of the Treres and Tilataeans.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Treres
snapshots.body: Who live north of Mount Scombrus and extend west as far as the Oskius.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Tilataeans
snapshots.body: Who live with the Treres north of Mount Scombrus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Sintians
snapshots.body: Divided from the Paeonians by the desolate range of Cercine, which Sitalces crossed by a road he had cut himself.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Maedians
snapshots.body: On Sitalces’s left as he crossed the mountains into Paeonia.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Lyncestae
snapshots.body: Macedonians by blood and allies and dependants of their kindred, but with their own separate government.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Elimiots
snapshots.body: Like the Lyncestae, Macedonians by blood with a government of their own.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Pierians
snapshots.body: Expelled from Pieria by Alexander’s ancestors and settled at Phagres beyond the Strymon; the coast they left is still called the Pierian gulf.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Eordians
snapshots.body: Driven out of Eordia, most of them killed, a few still living around Physca.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Almopians
snapshots.body: Driven out of Almopia by the same kings.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Temenids
snapshots.body: From Argos, the stock the kings of Macedonia came from.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Magnetes
snapshots.body: Subject to the Thessalians, and among the peoples who made their preparations when they heard how large Sitalces’s army was.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Panaeans
snapshots.body: One of the independent Thracian peoples of the plains beyond the Strymon who feared Sitalces might be invited against them.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Odomanti
snapshots.body: Independent Thracians of the plains beyond the Strymon.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Droi
snapshots.body: Independent Thracians of the plains beyond the Strymon.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Dersaeans
snapshots.body: Independent Thracians of the plains beyond the Strymon.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Scythians
snapshots.body: With whom, Thucydides says, no people in Europe can be compared, and no single nation in Asia is a match for them united — though they are not on a level with other races in general intelligence and the arts of civilized life.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Polichnitans
snapshots.body: Neighbours of the Cydonians, to oblige whom Nicias of Gortys got twenty Athenian ships diverted to Crete.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Cydonians
snapshots.body: Whose land the twenty ships and the Polichnitans laid waste instead of joining Phormio.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Anactorians
snapshots.body: Whose one ship joined the hundred and fifty at Sybota, and who marched into Acarnania with Cnemus and held the right with the Leucadians.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Tegeans
snapshots.body: Of Tegea in Arcadia. Timagoras, who travelled with the Lacedaemonian envoys to the King and was killed with them at Athens, was one of them.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Sicilians
snapshots.body: Whose tyrants had galleys before the Persian war; whose cities Lacedaemon ordered to build five hundred ships between them and to stay neutral meanwhile; and who in the end joined the enemies of Athens against her.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Abderites
snapshots.body: Nymphodorus, whose sister married Sitalces and who brought Athens the Thracian alliance, was one of them.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Plataeans
snapshots.body: Thebes’s old enemy and Athens’s oldest ally. Three hundred Thebans came into their town in the first watch of a rainy night; they dug through their own party walls to join up unseen, barricaded the streets with wagons, drove the Thebans into the mud and the dark, and killed a hundred and eighty of them. Besieged two years later, they answered the mound with a wooden wall, tunnelled out its footings, built a crescent behind it, snapped the battering rams with beams hung on chains, and came within a wind of being burnt alive. The siege closed on four hundred of their own citizens, eighty Athenians, and a hundred and ten women to bake the bread.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Athene
snapshots.body: On whose statue there were forty talents of pure gold, all of it removable — which Pericles counted among the city’s resources for a last extremity, to be used and paid back. The other deities’ temples are in the citadel with hers.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Demeter
snapshots.body: Whose Eleusinian temple was one of the few places kept closed when the country population camped in the city.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Dionysus
snapshots.body: Of the Marshes, in whose honour the older Dionysia are still held in Anthesterion — by the Athenians and by their Ionian descendants.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cleippides
snapshots.body: Deinias’s son, in command of the forty ships sent to catch the Mitylenians at the festival of the Malean Apollo outside the town — and, if that failed, to order them to give up their ships and pull down their walls.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Deinias
snapshots.body: Cleippides’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Meleas
snapshots.body: A Laconian who slipped into Mitylene by galley after the first battle and advised them to send more envoys to Lacedaemon.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hermaeondas
snapshots.body: A Theban, sent with Meleas before the insurrection and unable to get there before the Athenians.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Asopius
snapshots.body: Phormio’s son, whom the Acarnanians insisted on having because they would take no commander who was not some son or relative of Phormio — and who was cut off with most of his troops in the retreat from Nericus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Dorieus
snapshots.body: The Rhodian, in whose Olympiad — his second victory — the Mitylenian envoys made their case to the allies.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Alcidas
snapshots.body: The Lacedaemonian high admiral, and the most cautious man in the war. He took the relief fleet to Lesbos so slowly that Mitylene had fallen seven days before he heard of it; refused Teutiaplus’s advice to fall on Paches at night, refused the Ionian exiles’ advice to raise Ionia, butchered his prisoners at Myonnesus until Samian envoys told him this was no way to free Hellas, and fled home across the open sea. At Corcyra he would not attack the town even when Brasidas urged it. He was afterwards one of the three founders of Heraclea in Trachis.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Paches
snapshots.body: Epicurus’s son, who walled Mitylene in and took its surrender on terms — promising not to kill anyone until Athens had answered, and keeping it. He chased Alcidas as far as Patmos, trapped Hippias the Arcadian by a safe-conduct and shot him down inside his own fortification, and had the decree for the massacre in his hand when the second galley came into port.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Epicurus
snapshots.body: Paches’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Lysicles
snapshots.body: One of the five commanders of the twelve ships sent to levy subsidies from the allies, who went up country from Myus across the Meander plain to the hill of Sandius and was killed there with many of his men by the Carians and the people of Anaia. Not Abronichus’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Theaenetus
snapshots.body: Tolmides’s son, a soothsayer, who with Eupompides thought of the escape over the Peloponnesian wall at Plataea.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Tolmides
snapshots.body: Theaenetus the soothsayer’s father. Not Tolmaeus’s son.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Eupompides
snapshots.body: Daimachus’s son, one of the Plataean generals and joint author of the escape.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Daimachus
snapshots.body: Eupompides’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Ammias
snapshots.body: Coroebus’s son, first up the ladder and first on the Peloponnesian wall, at the head of twelve light-armed men with a dagger and a breastplate each.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Coroebus
snapshots.body: Ammias’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Androcrates
snapshots.body: The hero whose chapel the escaping Plataeans kept on their right, taking the Thebes road because it was the last one the pursuers would think of.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Salaethus
snapshots.body: The Lacedaemonian who got into Mitylene along a torrent bed, told them the fleet was coming, and stopped them treating with Athens — then armed the commons for a sortie, and lost the city the moment they had weapons in their hands. Found in hiding, sent to Athens and killed at once, though he offered to get the Peloponnesians away from Plataea.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cleomenes
snapshots.body: Who led the invasion of Attica in place of King Pausanias, his nephew, who was still a minor. Not the Cleomenes who drove the accursed out of Athens.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Pausanias
snapshots.body: Pleistoanax’s son and king of Lacedaemon, a minor when Cleomenes invaded Attica for him. Neither the regent nor the Macedonian.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Teutiaplus
snapshots.body: An Elean, who told Alcidas to sail straight for Mitylene and fall on it at night, since men who have just taken a city are as careless as any in war, and that detecting the moment when an enemy is at this disadvantage is what makes a successful general. Alcidas was not moved.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Itamenes
snapshots.body: Who took the upper town of Colophon with the barbarians, having been called in by one party in a quarrel.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Hippias
snapshots.body: Commander of the Arcadians in the fortified quarter at Notium, invited out to a parley by Paches on a promise of safe return, kept in custody, put back inside once the quarter had been stormed — as promised — and shot down as soon as he was in. Not the tyrant.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cleon
snapshots.body: Cleaenetus’s son, the most violent man at Athens and at that time by far the most powerful with the commons, who carried the decree to kill every adult male in Mitylene and enslave the rest, and defended it the next day: a democracy is incapable of empire, your empire is a despotism, pity and sentiment and indulgence are the three failings most fatal to it, and the penalty of rebellion must be death. He lost the second vote by a show of hands that was almost equal, and got the thousand prisoners killed instead.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Cleaenetus
snapshots.body: Cleon’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Diodotus
snapshots.body: Eucrates’s son, who answered Cleon by refusing to argue about guilt at all: the question is not justice but the interest of Athens, and no penalty yet invented has ever stopped men from taking a risk they have set their minds on — so killing the Mitylenian commons, who had surrendered the town the moment they got arms, would only teach every future rebel to hold out to the last. His motion carried, and the second galley beat the first by the length of a meal eaten at the oar.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Eucrates
snapshots.body: Diodotus’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.body: Who wanted to revolt before the war and were refused, and then had to do it before their walls and moles and archers were ready. snapshots.body: A volunteer proxenus of Athens and leader of the commons at Corcyra, acquitted on a charge of enslaving the city and answering it by prosecuting five rich men for cutting stakes in the ground sacred to Zeus and Alcinous. snapshots.body: Diitrephes’s son, who came up from Naupactus with twelve ships and five hundred Messenians and very nearly settled Corcyra: he got both parties to agree to try ten ringleaders, stopped the commons from killing men in the street, and persuaded four hundred suppliants out of the temple of Hera — and then sailed on.

snapshots.name: Eurymedon
snapshots.body: Thucles’s son, who came to Corcyra with sixty ships — and during the seven days he lay there the Corcyraeans went on butchering their fellow citizens, some for supposed conspiracy and some for money owed.

snapshots.name: Laches
snapshots.body: Melanopus’s son, who took twenty ships to Sicily with Charoeades, was left in sole command when Charoeades was killed, took Mylae and Messina, and was relieved by Pythodorus.

snapshots.name: The Dioscuri
snapshots.body: In whose temple at Corcyra the men enrolled for the ships sat down as suppliants, fearing they were to be sent to Athens.

snapshots.name: The Syracusans
snapshots.body: At war with Leontini, with all the Dorian cities of Sicily except Camarina for allies, and blockading the Leontines by land and sea when Athens first sent ships west.

snapshots.name: The Leontines
snapshots.body: Who had Camarina and the Chalcidian cities, and who appealed to Athens on their ancient alliance and their Ionian origin.

snapshots.name: The Rhegians
snapshots.body: Of Italy, who were for their Leontine kinsmen, and whose town the Athenians made their base.

snapshots.name: The Locrians of Italy
snapshots.body: Who were for the Syracusans, beat the Athenians at their fort on the Halex and again under Pythodorus, and were beaten on the Caicinus. Not the Ozolian or Opuntian Locrians of Greece.

snapshots.name: Agis
snapshots.body: Archidamus’s son, who brought the army as far as the Isthmus and turned back without invading because of the earthquakes.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Demosthenes
snapshots.body: Alcisthenes’s son. Talked by the Messenians into invading Aetolia against the Acarnanians’ advice, he pushed on without waiting for his Locrian darters, lost his archers’ captain and then his guide, and watched a hundred and twenty Athenian hoplites — by far the best men of the city to fall in the war — die in trackless gullies and in a wood the Aetolians burned around them. He stayed at Naupactus afraid to face Athens; and then saved Naupactus, hid four hundred men in a hollow road at Olpae, broke Eurylochus’s wing from behind, and destroyed the Ambraciot relief at Idomene at dawn by putting Messenians in front to speak Doric to the sentries.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Alcisthenes
snapshots.body: Demosthenes’s father.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Procles
snapshots.body: Theodorus’s son, Demosthenes’s colleague in the thirty ships, and among the slain in Aetolia.
